unit.title: Perform gas tungsten arc welding process to AWS specification (Pipe)

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to weld carbon steel and stainless steel pipe with gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW, or TIG) to a welding procedure specification (WPS) under the AWS code or procedure the Centre uses. You will learn how welder qualifications limit the work, how to prepare and fit up pipe, set up purging, and weld open roots, inserts, socket welds and butt joints in the 1G, 2G, 5G and 6G positions. You will also learn to inspect and test pipe welds, repair them, do the calculations, keep the records, and plan and lead a pipe job.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW)** of pipe to a written procedure: the welding of process, water, air and food lines where a leak or a failed weld can stop a plant, injure people or spoil a product. In Jamaican workshops GTAW is usually called **TIG** (tungsten inert gas) welding.

GTAW gives the cleanest, best-controlled root of any manual process, which is why so many pipe procedures use it for the root even when a faster process fills the joint. At this level you are expected to weld to the WPS, to check that you and the people you lead are qualified for the work, and to inspect, test and record it.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and welders moving into pipe work in factories, hotels, water and power plants, and on pipe fabrication jobs.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Work to the code and the WPS
Read the WPS, check that each welder's qualification (WPQ) covers the pipe sizes, wall thicknesses and positions, and keep inside the ranges.
Control high-frequency shocks, arc light, fume, argon build-up, hot pipe and pressure tests, and work safely in running plants.
Set up the DC power source, torch, cup, tungsten, shielding gas, purge equipment and filler for the job.
Check bevels, root face and gap, line the pipes up, tack them, set socket gaps and fit consumable inserts.
Set up dams and vents, purge to the oxygen level the WPS gives, and keep the purge on until the root has cooled.
Weld roots, hot passes, fills and caps in the 1G, 2G, 5G and 6G positions, and make socket and branch welds.
Inspect inside and out, know the tests (bend tests, radiography, penetrant, pressure tests), and repair faults to procedure.
Work out lengths, arc time, output, filler and gas; keep weld logs, weld maps and qualification records.
Read isometric drawings, number the welds, plan the order of work and the hold points, and brief and supervise the team.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on qualification, positions, inserts, socket welds, technique, root quality, purging, fit-up, filler, safety, orbital welding, calculations, inspection, testing, repairs, records and leading the team.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms or figures (for example welding operator, branch, cup, hold point, tie-in, bore, low-stress stamp, isometric, turning rolls, cerium, or a worked figure) and essays in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: a carbon steel pipe test coupon welded with GTAW in the 6G position to a WPS, with visual inspection, bend tests and a draft WPQ; and a small-bore pipe assembly with socket and butt welds, built from an isometric drawing, with penetrant checks and a weld log.

blocks.note: Questions at this level ask "which is best, and why?" and "what went wrong?". Learn what each setting and each step does to the root inside the pipe, because that is the part you cannot see and the part that fails.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Pipe work is done to a **code**: a published set of rules for design, welding, inspection and testing. The client's specification names the code. In this unit you work to the AWS code or procedure the Centre uses; other pipe jobs may name other codes, and the ideas are the same.

head: Document
What it is
rows: The written instructions for making the weld: process, pipe material and thickness range, diameter range, joint design, filler, tungsten, shielding and purge gas, current and polarity, positions and direction, preheat and interpass temperature, and technique
The record of the test weld that was made and tested to prove the WPS gives sound welds, with the actual settings used and the test results
The record that a welder passed a test, and the range of work it covers: process, positions, diameters, thickness, filler group and joint type
Shows that each welder has kept using the process, so the qualification stays current
A 3-D drawing of a pipe run, with sizes, fittings and every weld numbered
Links each weld number to its welder, WPS, filler batch, date and test results
Lists the checks and tests, and the hold points where work stops for the inspector

blocks.p: Each code lists **essential variables**. A change in one of them (for example the process, the pipe material group, a big change in thickness, the filler group, or removing the backing gas) needs a new or revised WPS, backed by a new PQR. Keeping inside the ranges on the WPS is the welder's job; checking it is the team leader's.

blocks.h: What a welder's pipe qualification covers

blocks.p: A welder qualifies by welding a test coupon that is inspected and tested. The WPQ then covers a range of work, worked out from the code's tables, and nothing outside it:

ul: **Process**: GTAW. If the test used GTAW for the root and MMAW for the fill, each process is qualified only for the thickness of weld metal the welder laid with it.
**Positions**: from the test position (see the next table).

**Diameter range**: from the code's table for the pipe size tested. A test on small-bore pipe generally covers larger pipe too, but a test on large pipe does not cover very small pipe, because on a tight curve the position changes much faster and is harder to control.
**Thickness**: the range of weld metal thickness the welder may lay, from the wall thickness tested.
**Filler group and joint type**: for example, an open root, a root on backing, or a root with a consumable insert.

head: Test position
How the pipe is set
Generally qualifies (check the code's table)
rows: Axis horizontal, pipe rolled; you weld on top
Axis vertical; the weld runs round horizontally
Axis horizontal and fixed; you weld up each side, through flat, vertical and overhead

blocks.note: A welder's qualification stays current only while they keep using the process: under most codes, a welder who has not welded with GTAW for a set period (often six months) must be re-tested. Check the continuity record as well as the certificate.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: In **orbital GTAW** a weld head clamps round the tube and turns the tungsten round the joint by itself, following a stored program of current, pulse and speed. The person who sets up and runs it is a **welding operator**, and must be qualified on that kind of equipment. A manual welder's WPQ does not cover it, and an operator's qualification does not cover manual welding.

Many pipe procedures use **GTAW for the root** and often the second pass, then **MMAW** (or another faster process) for the fill and cap. GTAW gives a clean, smooth, fully fused root, but lays metal slowly; MMAW fills a thick wall much faster. The WPS gives both processes and how thick the GTAW layer must be before the change. A second GTAW pass is usually laid so that the first MMAW run cannot burn through the thin root.

blocks.note: Never let a welder start on a joint that their WPQ does not cover. Check the qualifications when you plan the job, not after the radiographs come back.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Hazard
What can happen
Controls
rows: HF can jump to anyone touching the work, giving a sharp shock or a small, deep burn; it can upset computers, controls and other electronics nearby

Dry gloves; do not touch or steady the pipe with bare skin while starting; keep torch and work leads short and close together; warn plant staff and anyone with an implanted medical device; use lift-arc start near sensitive equipment
The GTAW arc gives off strong ultraviolet light that burns eyes and skin, and reflects off bright stainless steel
Helmet with the right shade (often about 10–12 for pipe GTAW; follow the chart); skin covered; screens for passers-by
UV light makes ozone; stainless steel fume contains chromium compounds
Extraction or good ventilation, more so in small plant rooms
Argon is heavier than air and has no smell. It collects in pits, trenches, low rooms, tanks and inside purged pipes, pushing out the oxygen, and can make you collapse without warning
Ventilate; never put your face to the open end of a purged pipe; vent purge gas away from people; follow confined-space rules
Red-banded (thoriated) tungsten is slightly radioactive; its grinding dust should not be breathed or swallowed
Use ceriated or lanthanated tungsten where the WPS allows; otherwise grind on a dedicated grinder with extraction and wash your hands
A falling cylinder can snap its valve; a damaged regulator can fail
Chain cylinders upright; close the valve after use; check hoses and regulators
Pipe stays hot long after the arc stops; a coupon or pipe can fall from a loose stand
Mark hot work HOT; use tongs; bolt or clamp test stands firmly and check them before starting
Lines may hold water, steam, fuel, chemicals or pressure
Isolate, lock off, drain and prove the line safe under a permit before cutting or welding
A failing joint under pressure can release water or gas with great force
Keep people clear while pressure is raised; never strike, tighten or weld on a line under pressure

flow: Get the permit to work and the hot work permit; agree the job with the plant's supervisor
Have the line isolated, locked off, drained and proven safe; release any trapped pressure
Clear or cover anything that can burn; put up screens; keep an extinguisher ready
Check ventilation, especially in small or low rooms where argon can collect
Warn plant staff about HF starting near control panels and computers
Weld, then keep a fire watch during and after the work and mark the hot pipe

blocks.note: Hotel plant rooms, water pumping stations and food factories are often small, hot and poorly ventilated. Plan breaks and drinking water, set up ventilation before you start, and treat any low pit or trench as a place where argon can gather.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: GTAW uses a **constant-current** power source. Carbon and stainless steel pipe are welded on **DC electrode negative (DCEN)**: the torch goes to the negative terminal and the work lead to the positive. Most of the heat then goes into the work and the tungsten stays cool and pointed.

Useful controls: **HF or lift-arc start**, **upslope** (current rises gently at the start), **downslope** (current falls gently at the end, to fill the crater), **pre-flow** and **post-flow** of gas, and **pulse** (the current switches between a high and a low value many times a second, helping to control heat on thin wall and out of position).
On pipe a foot pedal is rarely practical; a thumb or finger control on the torch, or set current with downslope, is usual.
Air-cooled torches suit lower currents; water-cooled torches suit long runs and higher currents. A short back cap helps in tight spaces.

head: Torch part
Its job
Points to know
rows: Directs the shielding gas over the weld
Sizes are numbered in sixteenths of an inch: a No. 6 cup is about 9.5 mm across inside, a No. 8 about 12.7 mm. Use the size the WPS gives.
Grip the tungsten and pass current to it
Must match the tungsten size; a loose collet overheats
A fine screen in place of the collet body that makes the gas flow smooth and even
Lets you stick the tungsten out further (for example into a deep groove or a tight root) and still keep good gas cover
Closes the back of the torch and holds the tungsten
Long, medium and short types for different access

head: Type
Usual colour band
Use
rows: Good general choice for DC on steel and stainless; easy starts at low current
Good general choice for DC; holds its point well
Traditional DC tungsten; slightly radioactive, so many shops now use the others
For AC on aluminium, not for steel pipe

ul: Common sizes for pipe are 1.6 mm, 2.4 mm and 3.2 mm; 2.4 mm is the most used.

For DCEN, grind a point with the grinding marks running **along** the tungsten, about 2 to 2½ times as long as the tungsten is thick, then leave a very small flat on the tip so it does not break off into the weld.
Use a wheel kept only for tungsten, so the tungsten does not pick up steel or other dirt.
If the tungsten touches the pool or the rod, stop. Grind out any tungsten left in the weld, and break off and re-grind the contaminated end before you carry on.

Shielding gas is usually welding-grade **argon**. The flow is set on a flowmeter, often about 8–15 L/min for pipe work, as the WPS says. Too much flow is as bad as too little: it becomes turbulent and drags air into the arc.
The **purge** (backing) gas inside the pipe is usually argon too, or another gas the WPS names. It protects the inside of the root (see the section on back purging).
Check hoses and connections for leaks: a leak can suck air into the gas.

head: Part of the code
In ER70S-2
What it tells you
rows: Can be used as an electrode (in GMAW) or a rod (in GTAW)
Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal: 70 000 psi (about 480 MPa)
The chemical make-up. ER70S-2 contains extra deoxidisers (aluminium, titanium and zirconium), so it gives sound welds even where the surface is not perfectly clean; it is a common choice for roots.

head: Pipe material
Usual filler (check the WPS)
rows: ER316L (it contains molybdenum, like the pipe, for resistance to pitting by salt and acids)

blocks.note: The "L" in 304L, 316L and ER316L means low carbon. Low carbon stops the metal next to the weld losing its resistance to corrosion. Keep rods in closed, labelled tubes, never mix stainless and carbon steel rods, wipe each rod clean, and snip off a rod end that has oxidised.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **consumable insert** is a ring of filler metal, of a set shape and of a grade to suit the pipe, placed in the root of the joint before welding. The root is then welded with GTAW, usually with little or no added rod: the insert and the pipe edges melt together and the insert becomes part of the weld. Inserts give a very even, smooth root profile inside, so a WPS may call for them on critical small-bore lines. The pipe ends are machined to the shape the insert needs; the insert is fitted to one end, the other pipe brought up tight, and the joint tacked through the insert.

ul: A programmable power source, and a weld head that clamps round the tube; closed heads hold the purge round the joint.

Thin-wall tube is often welded **autogenously** (with no filler), so the tube ends must be cut square, faced smooth, free of burrs and butted tight with no gap. The machine cannot see or correct a poor fit-up.
A test weld is usually made and checked at the start of each shift, and whenever the tube, the tungsten or the settings change.
Tube from different batches (heats) can weld slightly differently, so heat numbers are recorded.

blocks.p: Steel pipe is sold by **nominal size** (NPS in inches, or DN in millimetres) and **schedule**. Each nominal size has a fixed outside diameter; a higher schedule means a thicker wall and a smaller **bore** (the inside diameter).

head: Joint
Typical preparation (always follow the WPS)
Notes
rows: Bevel about 30–37.5° on each pipe; root face about 0–1.6 mm; root gap about 1.6–3 mm
The usual pipe butt joint; the root is welded from outside and must fuse right through
Square-cut ends butted tight, no bevel
Thin-wall tube, often stainless, often orbital
Ends machined to suit the insert, often a J shape with a land
Plain pipe end pushed into a socket fitting, then pulled back to leave a gap
A fillet weld round the outside; small-bore lines
Set-on: the branch sits on the main, over a hole the size of its bore. Set-in: the branch passes into a hole the size of its outside diameter
The joint angle changes all round the saddle shape

ul: Cut ends square with a pipe cutter, saw or bevelling machine; check with a wrap-around strip or square, and remove all burrs.
Check the bevel angle with a bevel gauge and file or grind the root face evenly all round.
Clean the bevels and about 25 mm inside and outside the pipe to bright metal. On stainless, use stainless brushes and a clean solvent, and keep it away from carbon steel dust.
Keep oily gloves off cleaned surfaces.

flow: Set the pipes on stands or V-blocks, or use an external line-up clamp
Set an even root gap all round, using a gap gauge or a piece of filler wire of the right size
Check the inside line-up with a **hi-lo gauge**: the step between the two bores must be inside the WPS or code limit (often about 1.5 mm or less, smaller on thin wall)
Check that the pipes are straight with a straight edge laid across the joint at several points
Tack at equal spacing: on small-bore pipe, usually three or four tacks (four tacks are 360° ÷ 4 = 90° apart). Each tack must be fully fused through the root
Grind each tack thin and taper both ends so the root can fuse right through it
Re-check the gap and line-up after tacking, because tacks shrink and can close the gap

blocks.note: If the gap is outside the WPS range, break the tacks and re-fit the joint. Do not try to fill a wide gap with extra rod or weld fast past it: the root will be faulty.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: For a socket weld, push the pipe fully into the socket, mark it at the socket face, then pull it back about **1.5 mm** and tack it. The gap lets the pipe grow as it heats and stops the pipe end pressing on the bottom of the socket; without it, the shrinking fillet is strained and can crack. Check after welding that the mark still shows the gap.

When you work out a cut length between two socket fittings, allow for the gap at each end. Pipe length = centre-to-centre distance − each fitting's centre-to-socket-bottom distance − the gap at each end.

ul: Pipe that has been in an air-conditioned store, or that carries cold water, is often colder than the air. In Jamaica's humid air, water droplets (dew) form on it, and they cause porosity. Warm the joint area gently (to about hand-warm) to drive the moisture off before welding.
Thicker pipe or alloy pipe may need a set **preheat** and a maximum **interpass** temperature; the WPS gives them. Check with temperature-indicating crayons or a contact thermometer.

blocks.p: When you weld a pipe root, the inside of the weld has no gas shield from the torch. On carbon steel this is usually accepted. On **stainless steel**, and on many alloy steels, the hot metal inside reacts with the air and forms a black, crusty, granular layer called **sugaring**. It has lost its resistance to corrosion, it is rough enough to trap dirt and bacteria in a food line, and it can hide lack of fusion. A **back purge** fills the inside of the pipe with argon (or the gas the WPS names) so the root cools in gas, not air.

flow: Fit dams inside the pipe on each side of the joint: water-soluble paper dams taped in place, inflatable purge bladders, or caps and plugs on short spools
Tape over the root gap on the outside, so gas does not escape through it; you peel the tape back a little at a time as you weld
Feed the purge gas in at the low end or side, and leave a vent at the high end: argon is heavier than air, so it fills from the bottom and pushes the air out of the top
Purge until an oxygen meter at the vent reads below the level the WPS gives, or for the time the WPS gives
Tack the joint only after the purge is established: tacks oxidise inside too
Turn the purge down to a gentle flow for welding, with the vent always open
Keep the purge running after the last pass until the root has cooled enough not to colour

blocks.note: Never seal a purged pipe completely. As the gas heats up, the pressure inside rises and can push the root inwards (a concave root) or blow the molten root out. Too strong a purge flow does the same.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The volume to fill between two dams is the area of the bore × the distance between the dams: V = π ÷ 4 × bore² × length. For example, a bore of 52.5 mm with dams 500 mm apart: 0.7854 × 5.25 cm × 5.25 cm × 50 cm ≈ 1 082 cm³, or about **1.1 litres**. Purges usually pass several times that volume before the oxygen falls low enough, which is why an oxygen meter is more reliable than a guess.

head: Inside colour of a stainless root
What it means
rows: Some oxygen got in; accepted on some jobs, not on others
Poor purge; usually rejected for corrosion or food service
No effective purge; rejected; the weld is cut out or the inside is repaired as the procedure says

blocks.note: Food, drink and pharmaceutical jobs often use a printed colour chart for the root, and check roots with a borescope (a small camera on a cable). Ask which chart the job uses before you start.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Argon inside a purged pipe or vessel can suffocate you. Never put your face to an open pipe end to look in, and never enter a vessel that has been purged until it has been ventilated and tested.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Hold a short arc, about the diameter of the tungsten or less.
Tilt the torch about 10–20° back from square, pointing in the direction of travel, and feed the rod into the front edge of the pool at a low angle. Keep the hot end of the rod inside the gas shield.
Add rod each time the pool flows; watch both edges of the joint melt before you move on.
On an open root, keep a small **keyhole** (a hole melted through at the front of the pool) to show that you are fusing right through.

head: Technique
How it works
When it helps
rows: The torch is held clear of the joint, the hand braced on the pipe or a rest
Most work, especially where the cup cannot touch
The cup rests on the bevel faces and is rocked from side to side, moving forward a little with each rock
Very steady arc length and travel on roots and fills; widely used on pipe
Rod is fed into the front of the pool from outside the pipe
Flat and vertical parts of the root
Rod is fed through the gap from inside, pushing filler up into the root
The overhead part of a fixed pipe, where the root tends to sag inwards
Rod is laid in the root and melted in as the arc travels along it
Tight gaps and a very even root

ul: To stop, use the **downslope** (or ease the current off), add a little rod as the pool shrinks to fill the crater, and hold the torch over the crater while the **post-flow** protects it.
Before you restart, grind the stop and the ends of every tack to a thin taper.
Restart on the taper, let the pool form, and carry the fusion through the taper. Joining a new run into an earlier one like this is called a **tie-in**.

head: Position
Technique
Watch for
rows: The pipe turns on rolls or by hand; you weld near the top, keeping the pool in the flat position. The quickest and easiest way to weld pipe
Matching the roll speed to a steady travel speed
Root with the torch tilted slightly up and the rod at the top edge; fill and cap with **stringer beads stacked from the bottom up**, each one overlapping about half of the one below
Sagging metal and undercut at the top edge
Weld each half uphill: start a little past the bottom (6 o'clock) and finish a little past the top (12 o'clock), then weld the other half, tying in at both ends
A root sunk in at the bottom (feed more rod, inside feed, less heat); too much penetration at the top (less heat, faster travel)
Root as for 5G; fill and cap with stringers laid from the **lower** side of the joint upwards, so each bead forms a shelf for the next
Sagging on the lower side; uneven cap

ul: The second pass (**hot pass**) protects the thin root and melts out small cold edges along it. In combination procedures it builds the GTAW layer to the thickness the WPS asks for before MMAW starts.
Clean every pass: wire-brush between passes (stainless brushes only on stainless), and grind any high spots.
Keep inside the interpass temperature limit; stainless pipe usually has a low limit, so let it cool.
Lay the cap so it overlaps each bevel edge by about 1–1.5 mm, with even reinforcement inside the code's limit and no undercut.
On large pipe, two welders often weld at the same time on opposite sides, so the heat goes in evenly and the joint stays in line.

Weld a socket fillet in the number of passes the WPS gives (often at least two), keeping the legs even on the pipe and on the fitting, and filling the crater. Aim a little more heat at the heavier fitting.
On a branch, the angle between branch and main changes all round the saddle, so change the torch and rod angles as you go. The WPS says whether the branch needs full penetration.

head: Fault
Likely causes
Cure
rows: Overhead section too hot; too little rod; purge pressure too high
Feed more rod (inside feed), less heat, lower purge flow with the vent open
Too much heat or rod, travel too slow, gap too wide; mostly at the top and flat parts
Less heat, faster travel, correct gap
Too little heat, root face too thick, gap too small, travel too fast
Correct fit-up; enough heat to keep the keyhole
Lack of fusion on one side
Torch aimed at, or heat favouring, the other side; misalignment
Aim the arc and rod so both edges melt; correct the line-up
Tungsten dipped in the pool or touched by the rod; current too high for the tungsten
Grind out; re-grind the tungsten; correct size and current
No purge, or purge not established, or air leaking in
Purge properly before tacking and welding; check dams and tape
Draughts, wrong gas flow, moisture on the pipe, dirt or oil
Screens, correct flow, warm off moisture, clean to bright metal
Arc stopped suddenly with the crater unfilled
Use the downslope and fill the crater

blocks.note: Excess penetration matters more in small-bore pipe than in large pipe: weld metal hanging inside narrows the bore and can block flow or trap dirt. Inside the pipe, the root should be smooth and even, with little protrusion.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Inspection before, during and after welding

head: Stage
What to check
rows: Material and size; bevel angle, root face and gap; inside line-up (hi-lo); cleanliness; tacks tapered; purge set up and reading right
Settings and gas inside the WPS ranges; root fused inside (check with a mirror or borescope where you can); cleaning between passes; interpass temperature
Cap: shape, reinforcement, undercut, arc strikes; root: penetration, concavity, colour; weld size on fillets; welder's ID marked; dimensions of the assembly

ul: Use good light, a mirror, a borescope, a bridge cam or other weld gauge, a fillet gauge and a hi-lo gauge.
A coupon or production weld that fails visual inspection has failed. It does not go on to bend tests or radiography to "see if it is really bad".
Whether a fault is acceptable is decided by the **inspector**, using the code's limits, not by the welder.

head: Test
What it finds
Points to know
rows: Surface faults, profile, size, root inside where visible
Always first; most rejects are found here
Cracks at and just below the surface
Internal faults: porosity, slag, lack of penetration, lack of fusion, tungsten inclusions
Film or digital; done by licensed, trained people behind barriers; often a set percentage of welds (spot) or all of them
Internal faults, especially flat ones such as lack of fusion
Used on thicker walls; trained operator
Lack of fusion, porosity and cracks opened up by bending

ul: Before the coupon leaves the stand, its top (12 o'clock) is marked. Strips are then cut from the places round the coupon that the code shows, so that each position is tested.
Thinner walls usually get **face** and **root** bends; thicker walls get **side** bends.
The cap and root are ground flush, the long edges are rounded, and each strip is bent round a former in a guided bend jig.
The bent strip passes if no open defect is larger than the code allows.

blocks.p: When only a percentage of welds is radiographed and one of them is rejected, most codes require **more welds by the same welder** (made at the same time, with the same WPS) to be examined, as the code sets out. If those fail too, the examination widens. This is why one bad weld can hold up a whole line, and why a welder who is struggling should be stopped early.
**Reject rate** = rejected welds ÷ welds examined × 100. For example, 3 rejects out of 40 radiographs is 3 ÷ 40 × 100 = 7.5%.

flow: Find the exact place and length of the fault from the report, the weld number and the film markers, and mark it on the pipe
Tell the supervisor; record the repair on the weld log; check that a repair WPS (or the original WPS) covers it
Grind the fault out from the outside, with tapered ends, until you reach sound metal; check by eye or with PT
On stainless, set up the purge again
Re-weld the cavity to the WPS, with a qualified welder, fusing well into the tapered ends
Inspect it visually and examine it again by the same method (for example radiograph it again)
Close the repair out on the records only when the new result is accepted

blocks.p: A finished line is usually **hydrostatically** tested: filled with water and pressurised to the test pressure in the specification (often 1.5 times the design pressure), then held while every weld is checked for leaks. Water is used because it hardly compresses, so it stores very little energy: if a joint fails, the pressure drops at once. Compressed air stores a great deal of energy and can burst a pipe violently, so a pneumatic test is used only when the specification calls for it, with extra precautions.

flow: Finish all welding and inspection first; close the system with rated blanks and isolate what must not be tested
Fill with clean water from the low point while opening vents at the high points to let all the air out
Raise the pressure slowly with a test pump, reading a calibrated gauge, with people kept clear
Hold for the set time and check every weld and joint for leaks
Let the pressure off slowly, drain, and record and sign the result

blocks.note: Never weld, grind or hammer on a line under pressure. If a weld leaks during the test, release the pressure and drain the line before any repair.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Study the isometrics: sizes, walls, materials, fittings and lengths; number every weld
List the joint types and positions; check there is a WPS for each and that every welder's WPQ and continuity cover them
Order pipe, fittings, filler, tungstens and gas; check mill certificates and mark heat numbers on cut pieces
Agree the inspection and test plan and the hold points with the client's inspector
Plan the order of work: make spools in the shop with as many welds as possible rolled (1G), leaving only the closing welds in fixed positions
Set up safe bays with screens, extraction and purge equipment
Brief the team; check fit-ups, settings and visual quality as the work goes on; keep the weld log
Finish tests and repairs; clean and cap the spools; complete the records for hand-over

blocks.note: A **hold point** is a stage where work must stop until the inspector has checked it, for example the fit-up of the first joints or the first production weld. If a welder goes past a hold point, stop the work and tell the inspector: the inspector decides what happens next.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Weld log or weld map**: weld number, welder, date, WPS, filler and its batch, inspection and test results, and any repairs.

**Welder's mark**: each welder marks their ID number beside the welds they make, so every weld can be traced. On pressure pipe, use **low-stress stamps** (with rounded characters) or a marker the specification allows; sharp stamps cut notches.
**Material traceability**: heat numbers from the mill certificate are carried onto every cut piece.
**Test records**: radiography and penetrant reports, bend test results, pressure test records.
**Storage**: filler rods in closed, labelled tubes; stainless and carbon steel kept apart; finished spools capped at both ends to keep dirt, water and insects out of the bore.

head: What you need
How
Worked example
rows: Length of one pass round a pipe
Joints ÷ (joints per welder per day × number of welders), rounded up
50 joints, 2 welders at 4 a day: 50 ÷ 8 = 6.25, so 7 days
Filler per joint × number of joints, plus a spare allowance
Centre to centre − both centre-to-socket-bottom distances − both gaps

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and check that the answer makes sense: a 114 mm pipe cannot have a 3 m circumference, and three welders cannot finish 90 joints in one day.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Give each welder only the joints their WPQ covers, and keep the continuity records up to date.
Brief the team on the WPS ranges, the purge set-up, the hold points and the safety controls, and check they understood.
Watch settings and technique. A welder who works outside the WPS because it "looks better" is stopped, the WPS is explained, and the welds already made are checked.
Keep the client's inspector informed, and never cover up a fault or a missed hold point.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain the WPS, PQR, WPQ, weld log and inspection and test plan, and what essential variables are.
I can check whether a welder's qualification covers a pipe job: process, positions, diameter, thickness and joint type.
I can name the pipe positions 1G, 2G, 5G and 6G and say what each generally qualifies.
I can explain orbital welding and why it needs a qualified welding operator and a perfect fit-up.
I can control HF, arc light, argon build-up, thoriated tungsten dust and the hazards of working in a running plant.
I can set up the power source, torch, cup, gas lens, tungsten and gas for pipe GTAW.
I can read a filler class such as ER70S-2 and choose filler for carbon steel and stainless pipe.
I can prepare, clean, line up and tack a pipe joint and check it with gauges.
I can set a socket-weld gap and work out a cut length between fittings.
I can set up and run a back purge and judge a stainless root by its colour.
I can weld roots, hot passes, fills and caps in 1G, 2G, 5G and 6G, with sound tie-ins.
I can name the common root faults and how to cure them.
I can inspect a pipe weld, explain bend tests, radiography and penetrant testing, and repair a rejected weld.
I can explain how a hydrostatic test is done safely.
I can do the job calculations and keep the weld log and traceability records.
I can plan a pipe job from the isometrics and lead a team through it.

terms: Back purge
Filling the inside of a pipe with gas so the root cools without touching air
Bore
The inside diameter of a pipe
Branch
A pipe joined onto the side of another pipe, forming a T
Combination procedure
A WPS that uses one process for the root and another for the fill and cap
Consumable insert
A ring of filler metal placed in the root and fused in to become part of the weld
Continuity
Evidence that a welder has kept using a process, so the qualification stays current
Cup (nozzle)
The part of the torch the shielding gas flows out of; sizes are numbered
DCEN
Direct current electrode negative: the torch on the negative terminal, used for steel and stainless
Downslope
A gradual fall in current at the end of a weld, to fill the crater
Gas lens
A screen in the torch that gives smooth gas flow, so the tungsten can stick out further
Hi-lo gauge
A gauge that checks the step between two pipe bores at a joint
Hold point
A stage at which work stops until the inspector has checked it
Hot pass
The pass laid over the root to protect it and melt out small faults
Hydrostatic test
A pressure test of a pipe system filled with water
Isometric drawing
A 3-D drawing of a pipe run, with every weld numbered
Keyhole
The small hole at the front of the pool that shows the root is fusing through
Low-stress stamp
A marking stamp with rounded characters that does not cut sharp notches
Orbital welding
Machine GTAW in which a weld head turns the tungsten round the tube
PQR
Procedure qualification record: the record of the test that proved a WPS
Schedule
A number that sets a pipe's wall thickness for its nominal size
Socket weld
A fillet weld joining a pipe end set in a socket fitting
Sugaring
The black, crusty oxide on an unpurged stainless root
Tie-in
Joining the end of one weld run into an earlier run or a tack
Turning rolls
A wheeled stand that turns a pipe under the torch for 1G welding
Walking the cup
Rocking the cup on the bevel faces to move the torch steadily along the joint
Weld log
The record that links each weld to its welder, WPS, filler and test results
Welding operator
A person qualified to set up and run automatic or orbital welding equipment
WPQ
Welder performance qualification: the record of a welder's test and what it covers
WPS
Welding procedure specification: the written instructions for making a weld

c1.title: Stainless product lines at a sauce factory in Kingston
c1.text: Jerome leads a team welding 316L stainless steel tube, 50.8 mm outside diameter with a 1.65 mm wall, for the product lines of a sauce factory in Kingston. The WPS calls for manual GTAW square butt joints, ER316L rod where filler is needed, argon shielding and an argon back purge, and says the purge must read below 0.05% oxygen before tacking. On the first joint the welder turned the purge on and struck the arc almost at once, and the root inside came out black, crusty and rough.

c2.title: A 6G qualification test in Mandeville
c2.text: Kerry-Ann is taking a GTAW pipe qualification test at a training centre in Mandeville, Manchester. Her coupon is carbon steel pipe, 60.3 mm outside diameter with a 5.5 mm wall, fixed at 45° in a 6G stand. The WPS calls for ER70S-2 rod, DCEN and a 2.4 mm 2% ceriated tungsten. Partway up the root, her tungsten touches the weld pool. Later, one of her root bend strips cracks open at the root, and the two original root faces can be seen, unmelted, in the middle of the crack.

c3.title: Socket welds on an air header in Old Harbour
c3.text: Omar is welding a compressed-air header for a power plant in Old Harbour, St Catherine, from DN 25 carbon steel pipe and forged socket-weld fittings. The WPS calls for GTAW with ER70S-2 rod, at least two passes, and fillet legs of at least 6 mm. The isometric gives 450 mm, centre to centre, between two fittings; each fitting measures 22 mm from its centre to the bottom of its socket. Omar's helper wants to push each pipe hard against the bottom of its socket "so it is strong".

c4.title: A pumping-station main in Port Morant
c4.text: A contractor is replacing pipework at a water pumping station in Port Morant, St Thomas: carbon steel pipe 168.3 mm across with a 7.1 mm wall. The WPS uses GTAW for the root and second pass, and E7018 electrodes (MMAW) for the fill and cap. Ten per cent of the welds are radiographed. Two of the first films show lack of fusion in the root, both on welds by the same welder. The finished line will then be pressure tested with water.

c5.title: Planning pipe skids near Lionel Town
c5.text: Andrea is planning the GTAW welding of carbon steel pipe skids for a factory near Lionel Town, Clarendon. There are 96 butt joints in 114.3 mm pipe, and most of the spools can be welded on turning rolls in the shop. Each joint needs about 70 minutes of arc time at an argon flow of 10 L/min, and the shop's argon cylinders hold about 9 000 litres each. One of her three welders, Leon, last welded with GTAW eight months ago.

questions.q: Why did the first root come out black, crusty and rough?
o: The torch's argon flow was set far too low for the cup size
The purge had not yet pushed the air out of the tube
The tube wall was too thin for a square butt joint like this
ER316L rod cannot be used on 316L stainless tube
questions.why: The inside of the root is shielded only by the purge. Air must be pushed out until the oxygen reading meets the WPS before tacking or welding; striking the arc at once left the hot root in air, and it oxidised (sugared).

questions.q: Once the purge reads below 0.05% oxygen, what should be done with the purge while the joint is welded?
o: Turn it up high so that no air can leak back in
Close the vent so that the argon cannot escape
Turn it down to a gentle flow with the vent open
Switch it off, since the tube is now full of argon
questions.why: A gentle flow keeps the inside shielded without building pressure. A high flow, or a closed vent, lets pressure rise as the gas heats, which pushes the root inwards or blows it out; with no flow, air soon leaks back in.

questions.q: The tube's bore is 47.5 mm and the purge dams are 600 mm apart. About how much gas fills the space between them once?
o: About 0.3 litres
About 1.1 litres
About 4.3 litres
About 11 litres
questions.why: Volume = π ÷ 4 × bore² × length = 0.7854 × 4.75 cm × 4.75 cm × 60 cm ≈ 1 063 cm³, about 1.1 litres. Using the whole diameter in place of the radius in π × r² gives the wrong 4.3 litres.

questions.q: Why does the WPS call for ER316L rod rather than ER308L on these lines?
o: ER308L cannot be used with pure argon shielding gas
ER316L is stronger, so fewer passes are needed overall
ER308L is made only for welding stainless on AC
It has molybdenum, like 316L, to resist pitting
questions.why: 316L contains molybdenum, which helps it resist pitting by salt and acids, as in sauces. ER316L matches it, so the weld is as corrosion-resistant as the tube; ER308L suits 304 stainless.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do after her tungsten touches the weld pool?
o: Carry on, as the arc will soon burn the tungsten clean
Turn the current up so the tungsten melts into the root
Stop, grind out the spot and re-prepare the tungsten
Fit a larger cup and carry on welding up the root
questions.why: A dipped tungsten leaves tungsten in the weld, which shows on a radiograph and weakens the root, and the contaminated tungsten gives an unstable arc. Stop, grind out the contaminated spot, break off and re-grind the tungsten, then restart on a taper.

questions.q: What fault does the cracked root bend strip show?
o: Incomplete penetration: the root faces never fused
Lack of side-wall fusion in the cap and fill passes
Porosity from a draught blowing across the stand
Undercut along the toe of the cap on the outside
questions.why: Seeing the original root faces means the arc never melted right through the root. Causes include a gap that was too small, a root face that was too thick, too little heat, or not keeping a keyhole.

questions.q: If Kerry-Ann passes, which positions does a 6G pipe test generally qualify her for?
o: Pipe fixed at 45° only, as tested
Flat and horizontal positions only
All positions, within the code's limits
Vertical and overhead pipe positions only
questions.why: The 6G position takes in flat, vertical, horizontal and overhead welding in one coupon, so it generally qualifies all positions. The diameter and thickness ranges still come from the code's tables.

questions.q: Why is ER70S-2 a common choice of rod for carbon steel pipe roots like hers?
o: Its extra deoxidisers give sound welds on less-clean surfaces
It has a flux core that protects the inside of the root from the air
It is a low-strength rod, so the root bends easily in the bend test
It contains chromium, which stops the inside of the pipe rusting
questions.why: ER70S-2 contains aluminium, titanium and zirconium as well as manganese and silicon, which deal with oxygen and some surface contamination, giving a sound root. It is a solid rod with no flux, and its 70 means 70 000 psi minimum tensile strength.

questions.q: How should Omar set each pipe in its socket before tacking?
o: Push it fully home, then tack it tight against the bottom
Push it in until it is about half way into the socket
Push it fully home, mark it, then pull it back 1.5 mm
Push it in, then pack the bottom of the socket with rod
questions.why: The gap at the bottom of the socket lets the pipe expand as it heats and stops the shrinking fillet being strained against the socket bottom, which can crack it. The mark shows afterwards that the gap was kept.

questions.q: What length should Omar cut the pipe between the two fittings?
o: 450 mm
406 mm
403 mm
409 mm
questions.why: Take off both centre-to-socket-bottom distances and both gaps: 450 − 22 − 22 − 1.5 − 1.5 = 403 mm. Forgetting the gaps gives 406 mm, and the pipe would then sit hard against the socket bottoms.

questions.q: A penetrant check on one socket weld shows a sharp red line along the toe on the pipe side. What does it most likely show?
o: Normal staining that can be wiped off before passing it
Porosity, which is accepted because the pores are small
Too much developer, so more is sprayed and it is re-read
A crack or unfused toe, so the weld is repaired
questions.why: In a penetrant test a sharp, continuous red line shows a crack or a lack of fusion open to the surface; round dots show pores. The fault is ground out, re-welded to the WPS and tested again.

questions.q: During the line's pressure test, one socket weld weeps. What must happen before it is repaired?
o: The pressure is let off and the line drained
The pressure is kept on so the leak shows while welding
The leaking weld is hammered to close up the pores
The test pump is stopped but the pressure left on
questions.why: Welding, grinding or hammering on a line under pressure can make it fail violently, and water in the line spoils the weld. Release the pressure, drain the line, repair to procedure, and test again.

questions.q: Two spot-checked welds by the same welder have failed. What does the code usually require next?
o: Only the two faulty welds are repaired, and nothing more
More welds by that welder are examined, as the code sets out
All the welds are cut out and remade by another welder
The welder's welds are passed if the water test shows no leak
questions.why: A rejected spot radiograph suggests other welds by that welder may have the same fault, so codes call for extra welds of the same kind by the same welder to be examined; if those fail, the examination widens.

questions.q: Why does the WPS call for a second GTAW pass before the first E7018 run?
o: So the E7018 slag cannot stick to the GTAW root
So the radiographer can tell the two processes apart
So the welder can rest between the two processes
So the first E7018 run cannot burn through the root
questions.why: A single GTAW root is thin, and an E7018 run puts in much more heat and force. A second GTAW pass builds up the thickness so the first MMAW run cannot burn through or reheat the root into faults.

questions.q: Why are the vents at the high points left open while the line is filled for the water test?
o: So all the air is let out as the line fills
So the gauge reads the highest pressure in the system
So the water drains out faster once the test is done
So the inspector can look inside the pipe during the test
questions.why: Trapped air compresses and stores energy, which is what makes a failure violent, and it makes the gauge reading unsteady. Filling from the low point with high-point vents open lets all the air out first.

questions.q: About how many 9 000 L argon cylinders will the shielding gas for all 96 joints need, before any allowance for purging or leaks?
questions.why: Each joint uses 10 L/min × 70 min = 700 L; 96 × 700 = 67 200 L. 67 200 ÷ 9 000 = 7.5, so 8 cylinders are needed: 7 would run out before the job ends.

questions.q: What should Andrea do about Leon before giving him any joints?
o: Let him weld, as his WPQ certificate shows no expiry date
Let him weld roots only, with another welder watching him
Let him weld once he has practised on scrap for a day
Check his continuity record, as he may need to requalify
questions.why: Under most codes a welder who has not used the process for a set period (often six months) must be re-tested before production work. Eight months without GTAW means his qualification has probably lapsed.

questions.q: Why should Andrea plan for as many joints as possible to be welded on the turning rolls?
o: Rolled (1G) welds are quicker and easier to do well
Rolled welds do not need a WPS or a qualified welder
Rolled welds do not need inspecting or radiographing
Rolled welds use no filler rod at all on the root pass
questions.why: On rolls the welder stays in the flat position while the pipe turns, so welding is faster and quality is easier to keep. Only the closing welds then need fixed-position work; every weld still needs a WPS, a qualified welder and inspection.

questions.q: A welder is grinding red-banded tungstens on the general bench grinder. What is the main concern?
o: Red-banded tungstens shatter if they are ground too fast
Its grinding dust is slightly radioactive if breathed
The red band shows the tungsten is only for AC welding
Grinding removes the coating that makes the arc start
questions.why: Red-banded tungsten is thoriated, and thorium is slightly radioactive. Grind it on a dedicated grinder with extraction, wash your hands, or use ceriated or lanthanated tungsten where the WPS allows; a shared wheel also contaminates the tungsten.

questions.q: What does fitting a gas lens to a GTAW torch let a pipe welder do?
o: Use pure tungsten on DC without its tip balling up
Extend the tungsten further and keep gas cover
Weld stainless pipe without needing any back purge
Strike the arc without high-frequency starting
questions.why: A gas lens smooths the gas flow so it stays even further from the cup. The welder can then extend the tungsten into a deep groove or tight root and still shield the pool; it does nothing for the inside of the pipe.
